newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs, Germans set to apologise over WW2.
newsitem.headline: Czechs, Germans set to apologise over WW2.

text.p: Germany and the Czech Republic will apologise to each other for Nazi war crimes and Czech excesses after World War Two against ethnic Germans in a joint declaration, according to a draft of the document obtained by Reuters on Monday.

In the long-awaited declaration, Bonn strongly backs Czech ambitions to join the European Union (EU) and NATO defence alliance. The declaration also calls for a fund aimed mainly at compensating Czech victims of the Nazi occupation.
Diplomats said few changes to the document, if any, would be made.
The draft is expected to be initialled by Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec and his German counterpart, Klaus Kinkel on December 20 in Western Bohemia.

The next step is for the prime ministers to sign the document and diplomats expect German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to visit his Czech counterpart Vaclav Klaus in Prague in late January. Finally it will be ratified by both parliaments.

In the declaration, Bonn apologises for Nazi brutality during the occupation of the former Czechoslovakia while Prague admits that innocent people suffered injustice when the country's 2.5 million Sudeten German minority was expelled en masse after World War Two.
Czech and German negotiators have laboured for about two years to complete the declaration, which aims to close the book on 50 years of mistrust following the war.

Zieleniec told the Czech news agency CTK that leaked copies of the text, which originally appeared on the German Television station ARD, appeared to be authentic. He said he was sorry the text was originally leaked by one side because he hoped it would presented to the Czech and German public jointly.

But he added "the text clearly shows that it is balanced and that its main task is to turn Czech-German relations toward the future." It was important to emphasise that neither side would be burdened by past legal and political questions, he said..
Many of the delays have been due to objections to the text from Sudeten German groups mostly based in Bavaria.
Bonn admits that the Nazi occupation, which began with Hitler's annexation of areas where the Sudetens were in a majority, laid the foundation for the mass expulsions.

"The German side...is aware of the fact that the National Socialist policy of violence against the Czech people helped to create the basis for the post-war escape, expulsion and forced resettlement," the draft says.
Bonn also admits German responsibility in the 1938 Munich pact when Britain and France let Adolf Hitler annex Sudetenland, believing it would satisfy his territorial ambitions.
Within months, the Nazis had overrun the rest of the Czech lands and set up a puppet state in Slovakia in the prelude to conquering much of Europe.

Prague insists that the expulsions, in which Sudetens were hounded from their homes, stripped of their property and expelled to Germany, were legal and authorised by the victorious allies at the 1945 Potsdam conference.

But Czech President Vaclav Havel, a prime mover behind the declaration, has apologised for the indiscriminate nature of the expulsions. A Sudeten minority stayed loyal to the Czechoslovak state, a prosperous democracy before the Nazi occupation.
